top_story: Missile strikes that sank two container ships near the Strait of Hormuz on 14 October marked the most destabilizing shift, sharpening pressure on a maritime chokepoint that underpins regional trade and exposing Gulf societies to higher economic risk through insurance, shipping disruption, and price volatility. A day later, researchers tied an Israeli spyware capability to zero-click ad delivery that could reach vast numbers of devices, showing how regional coercion now extends beyond borders and battlefields into routine digital life, including the surveillance of journalists and civilians. On 16 October, Saudi Arabia’s move toward executing a man for protest-related acts allegedly committed at age 15 reinforced a parallel pattern of hardline state control at home, where political dissent and even collective mourning carry life-and-death consequences. Together, these developments point to a regional environment in which governments and allied security actors are expanding the means of coercion across sea lanes, screens, and courts, deepening insecurity for ordinary people as much as for states.
